note: Offline seed corpus for The Dead Web Gazette.
Every fact carries a confidence level (high = attested by multiple canonical
records; medium = widely reported but numbers/details vary, use hedged wording)
and a canonical source URL for human verification. Per the truthfulness law,
medium-confidence facts must appear hedged in posts, never as bare assertions.
This is a distilled fact sheet collection, not a raw data dump.

facts.text: Founded in 1994 as Beverly Hills Internet by David Bohnett and John Rezner.
Organized user homepages into themed virtual neighborhoods with street-style addresses.
Renamed GeoCities in 1995.
Hosted millions of user-built pages; by the late 2000s the count was reported in the tens of millions.
Acquired by Yahoo! in 1999 in a stock deal reported at the time at roughly 3.6 billion US dollars.
Yahoo! announced the shutdown in April 2009 and closed the US service on October 26, 2009.
Before closure, volunteer archivists including Archive Team raced to mirror millions of pages; a substantial portion survives in the Internet Archive.
Released in June 1999, built by Shawn Fanning with Sean Parker.
Popularized peer-to-peer file sharing for music, connecting strangers' hard drives directly.
By 2000-2001 the service was reported to have tens of millions of registered users.
Sued by the major-record-label trade group in December 1999 (A&M Records v. Napster).
facts.source: Wikipedia: A&M Records, Inc. v. Napster, Inc.

facts.text: After adverse court rulings, Napster shut its service down in July 2001.
Filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in 2002; the brand was later sold and resurfaced on legal music services under other owners.
Launched on October 7, 2005 through Google Labs as an RSS feed reader.
Became the center of gravity for a devoted community of readers who shared and annotated items.
Google announced its retirement on March 13, 2013, in a blog post framed as a round of spring cleaning.
The service was retired on July 1, 2013.
The shutdown was widely covered and gave a lasting boost to alternatives such as Feedly, by most accounts in the tech press.
Created in 2003 by Joshua Schachter; pioneered social bookmarking and popularized tagging.
Acquired by Yahoo! at the end of 2005.
An internal Yahoo! slide leaked in December 2010 suggesting the service would be sunset, triggering user panic and mass exports.
Sold to AVOS Systems, a company of YouTube founders Chad Hurley and Steve Chen, in 2011.
Acquired by Pinboard on June 1, 2017 and placed in read-only mode as an archive.
Founded in 2002 by Jonathan Abrams as one of the first mainstream social networks.
By the late 2000s it claimed well over one hundred million registered users, most of them in Asia.
In 2011 it relaunched as a social gaming service and deleted users' stored photos, blogs, and comments ahead of the switch.
The remnant service closed in 2015.
First released in April 1997, written by Justin Frankel under the Nullsoft name.
Its skinnable interface made it the default MP3 player of the late 1990s.
Nullsoft was acquired by AOL in 1999 in a deal reported at the time at roughly 80 to 100 million US dollars.
AOL announced in October 2013 that Winamp would be shut down that December.
Instead the brand was sold to Radionomy, announced in January 2014.
The player shipped a famous spoken tagline: it really whips the llama.
Launched on July 22, 1999 as MSN Messenger.
Renamed Windows Live Messenger in the mid-2000s as part of the Windows Live wave.
Defined an era of after-school chatting: buddy lists, nudges, custom emoticons, and songs displayed in status messages.
Microsoft retired it in most markets in 2013 in favor of Skype.
Mainland China kept the service until October 31, 2014, the last region to go dark.
Launched on December 15, 1995 out of research at Digital Equipment Corporation.
Stunned the mid-90s web with full-text search over what was then an enormous index, reported in the tens of millions of pages.
Passed through a chain of owners, including Compaq and Overture, before ending up under Yahoo!.
Yahoo! shut AltaVista down on July 8, 2013.
Launched by AOL in 1997.
The buddy list defined a generation of evening internet use in the United States.
AOL announced in October 2017 that the service would end, and it went dark on December 15, 2017.
Launched in August 2003.
Acquired by News Corporation in July 2005 for 580 million US dollars.
In 2006 it was reported by at least one major measurement firm as the most-visited website in the United States.
Customizable profile pages with embedded music became its signature.
Sold in June 2011 to Specific Media for a price reported at around 35 million US dollars.
Founded in 2001 by Garrett Camp and co-founders while he was a student.
A toolbar whose Stumble button sent you to a random page matched to your interests.
Shut down on June 30, 2018, with users directed to its successor, Mix.
Launched in December 2004 by Kevin Rose and partners.
Community voting pushed stories to the front page; a front-page hit could flatten smaller sites, the so-called Digg effect.
The August 2010 version 4 redesign triggered a user revolt and a mass exodus to rival Reddit.
Sold to Betaworks in July 2012 for a price reported at around half a million US dollars, a fraction of the venture capital it had raised.
Launched in 2008 by Sachin Agarwal; let you blog by sending email.
Acquired by Twitter in March 2012.
Twitter announced in 2013 that Posterous would close on May 31, 2013, and offered backup tools.
An online pet-supplies store founded in 1998, selling bags of kibble by courier.
Its sock-puppet mascot starred in a Super Bowl advertisement in January 2000.
Went public in February 2000 at the top of the dot-com wave.
Announced liquidation in November 2000, roughly nine months after its IPO.
Became shorthand in business writing for dot-com excess.
An online toy retailer that went public in May 1999 at the height of the dot-com boom.
Filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in March 2001.
The etoys.com address later ended up under other retail owners.
Launched in January 2013 by Twitter, which had acquired the startup in 2012.
Built an entire comedy and music culture out of six-second looping videos.
Twitter announced in October 2016 that the app would be discontinued; it was wound down into a stripped-down camera app in January 2017.
Launched on June 28, 2011 as Google's answer to Facebook.
The consumer version was shut down on April 2, 2019, after Google disclosed a software flaw that had exposed profile data and acknowledged low usage.
Founded in 1999 by Rich Kyanka as a comedy website.
Its pay-to-register forums incubated large chunks of early internet culture and memes.
Kyanka died in November 2021, as widely reported at the time.
The forums continue to operate today.
Created in 1995 by Tom Fulp.
Became the hub of the Flash animation and browser-game scene of the early 2000s.
Widely credited as a springboard for Flash-era animators and game makers.
A search engine launched in July 2008 by former Google engineers, with massive press coverage at launch.
Claimed an index of roughly 120 billion web pages, far more than competitors publicly admitted to.
The site stumbled badly on launch day under its own traffic, and closed in September 2010, a little over two years later.
